```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
```

## The Problem

Quick question. In one place, 2.4 out of every 100 hospital patients
catch an infection during their stay. In another, it's 2.8. Which one
has the bigger problem?

The second, surely. And on the surface, it's not wrong, fewer patients getting infected *does* sound like the safer, better-performing system.

But when I looked a little deeper, the answer flipped. The first place is Germany, the second is the European average, and by one important measure, Germany actually came out *worse*.

Some patients pick up a new infection while they're in hospital, such as
pneumonia, a bloodstream infection or a urinary tract infection. These
are called **healthcare-associated infections**. But not all infections
are equal. A urinary tract infection is common but usually mild, while a
bloodstream infection is rarer but can be deadly. So researchers measure
harm a different way.

::: callout-note
## What's a DALY?

A **disability-adjusted life year (DALY)** is one year of healthy life
lost, whether from dying early or living with illness. It lets us
compare a common, mild infection with a rare, deadly one on the same
scale.
:::

That leaves two questions:

1. **Which infections cause the most harm?**
2. **If German patients are less likely to get infected, how can Germany lose more healthy life?**

## What the evidence shows

### Where the data comes from

@zacher2019 used a one-day survey of **9,626 patients in 46 German hospitals** from 2011, chosen to represent hospitals of different sizes. 

They compared it with the same survey run across 29 European countries in 2011–2012, covering more than 273,000 patients. To turn these surveys into
estimates of harm for a whole country, they built a free tool called BHAI.[^bhai]

[^bhai]: BHAI stands for "Burden of Healthcare-Associated Infections". It's an R package anyone can download from CRAN.

But how *common* an infection is and how much *harm* it causes are two very different things.

In @fig-share, each arrow starts at an infection's share of cases and ends at its share of theharm. Bloodstream infections are only about 6% of cases but cause almost a quarter of the harm.Urinary tract infections are the opposite: nearly half of all cases, but only about a quarter of the harm. Together, pneumonia and bloodstream infections make up just 28% of cases but about half of all healthy life lost.


```{r}
#| label: fig-share
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Each arrow runs from an infection's share of cases to its share of the harm (healthy years of life lost). Blue arrows mark infections that cause more harm than their case numbers suggest; C. difficile causes about the same share of each."
#| fig-alt: "Arrow chart for five infection types in Germany, 2011. Bloodstream infection rises from 6% of cases to 23% of harm and pneumonia from 22% to 28%. Urinary tract infection falls from 45% of cases to 27% of harm and surgical site infection from 19% to 12%. C. difficile is about 8% of both."
#| echo: false

# Annual estimates for Germany, 2011 (Zacher et al. 2019, Table 1)
infections <- tribble(
  ~infection,                ~cases,  ~dalys,
  "Pneumonia",               106586,  69508,
  "Urinary tract infection", 214150,  66701,
  "Bloodstream infection",    26976,  58350,
  "Surgical site infection",  93222,  28842,
  "C. difficile infection",   36002,  20890
)

plot_data <- infections |>
  mutate(
    cases_pct = cases / 478222 * 100,
    harm_pct  = dalys / 248920 * 100,
    more_harm = harm_pct > cases_pct,
    same      = abs(harm_pct - cases_pct) < 1,   # less than 1 point apart
    infection = fct_reorder(infection, harm_pct)
  )

changed <- filter(plot_data, !same)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(y = infection)) +
  # Arrows only where the share really changes
  geom_segment(
    data = changed,
    aes(x = cases_pct, xend = harm_pct, yend = infection, colour = more_harm),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")), linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = cases_pct), colour = "grey50", size = 3) +
  # Share of cases (grey)
  geom_text(aes(x = cases_pct,
                label = if_else(same,
                                paste0(round(cases_pct), "% of both (about the same)"),
                                paste0(round(cases_pct), "%")),
                hjust = case_when(same ~ -0.1, more_harm ~ 1.4, TRUE ~ -0.4)),
            colour = "grey40", size = 3.5) +
  # Share of harm (coloured)
  geom_text(data = changed,
            aes(x = harm_pct, label = paste0(round(harm_pct), "%"),
                hjust = if_else(more_harm, -0.4, 1.4), colour = more_harm),
            size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2a5d8f", "FALSE" = "#a89c88")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 52), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Some infections cause far more harm\nthan their case numbers suggest",
    subtitle = "Dot = share of cases, arrowhead = share of healthy life lost",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption  = "Source: Zacher et al. (2019), Germany, 2011"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position     = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y  = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor    = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.title          = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption        = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey40")
  )
```

### How can "safer" Germany lose more?

@tbl-compare shows how the answer flips depending on which number you look at.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Germany has a lower infection rate among hospital patients than the EU/EEA average, but more infections and more healthy life lost across its whole population. Which looks better depends on the number you choose."

tribble(
  ~Measure,                                   ~Germany, ~`EU/EEA`, ~`Looks better`,
  "Infections per 100 hospital patients",      "2.40",   "2.83",    "Germany",
  "Infections per 100,000 people",             "592.1",  "467.9",   "EU/EEA",
  "Healthy years lost per 100,000 people",     "308.2",  "290.0",   "EU/EEA"
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lccc")
```

Think of it like two roads. On Road A, 3 in every 100 cars crash, but only 1,000 cars use it eachday, so that's **30 crashes**. Road B is safer: only 2.4 in every 100 cars crash. But it's a busy highway with 3,000 cars a day, so that's **72 crashes**. Road B is the safer road *per car*, yet
it still has more crashes overall, simply because so many more cars drive on it.

Germany is Road B. Each patient's chance of catching an infection is lower (the crash rate), but far more people go into hospital (the traffic), so the total harm across the country (the number of crashes) ends up higher.


::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## How sure can we be? (click to expand)
These numbers are estimates, and some are quite uncertain. Germany's harm could be anywhere from
about 221 to 416 healthy years lost per 100,000 people, and Europe's from about 215 to 377. Those
ranges overlap, so the study can't say for certain that Germany is really worse.

The authors also note that some of the evidence linking infections to deaths and disability is
weak, and that using a different group of German hospitals raised the total from about 249,000 to
290,000 healthy years lost.
:::

## Conclusion: question the numbers you see

So, which infections do the most harm? Pneumonia and bloodstream infections: only about a quarterof cases, but half of all the healthy life lost. And how can "safer" Germany lose more? Because arate among hospital patients and a total across a whole country answer different questions, andGermany's large hospital population may tip the balance [@zacher2019].

What stuck with me is how many times the story changed as I kept looking. Count cases, and urinary tract infections look like the biggest problem. Compare hospital rates, and Germany looks like a success. Measure healthy life lost, and Germany looks worse. Check the uncertainty, and even that
difference might not be real.


::: {.callout-tip}
## How to question a number
- **Ask what's being counted.** Cases, deaths and years of healthy life are different things.
- **Ask "out of how many?"** A good rate across a big group can still mean a big total.
- **Check how sure it is.** A precise-looking number can hide a wide range.
- **Separate "likely" from "proven".** A suggested reason isn't a confirmed cause.
:::


Next time a statistic looks obvious, pause and question it. It might be answering a different question from the one you actually care about.
